reasons: [reasoning_validity/major] D1 [verdict; C3 assessment; alternatives (Compute SP, EC2 Instance SP); counterarguments #2; tradeoffs #1; K5] The main recommendation is to prefer a Compute SP over the m7i-locked EC2 Instance SP, but the draft's own numbers do not back it. Committed spend under the Compute SP is 0.0511/0.0457 = 1.118, so it costs about 11.8% more for the same m7i usage. The draft calls this 'about 5.4 percentage points' (K5), which makes the premium sound smaller than it is. The hedge also buys little. If the workload moves to M8i and the Compute SP gives the same percentage discount, the cost per m7i-equivalent of performance is about 0.0511*1.05/1.2 = 0.0447/hr. A locked EC2 Instance SP costs 0.0457/hr. That is a gain of about 2%, set against paying about 12% more for every hour before migration. Graviton (m7g at $0.0816, so about 0.0414 under a Compute SP at the same discount) changes the picture only modestly. The draft never weighs migration timing or likelihood against the premium. It asserts that the flexible plan 'avoids being locked' without showing that the flexibility is worth the price. On these figures the EC2 Instance SP may well come out ahead unless the workload changes family, region or OS, or moves to Fargate or Lambda.

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [C3 assessment; K22] In C3 the draft argues that an m7i lock is 'more of an opportunity cost than an outright loss' by comparing the locked m7i rate ($0.0457) with M8i ON-DEMAND (K22, about $0.088). That is the wrong comparison. The real alternative to a locked EC2 Instance SP is M8i under a commitment (Compute SP or an M8i EC2 Instance SP), which costs about $0.045 per m7i-equivalent. Against that alternative the two are nearly equal. The comparison chosen is a strawman, and it tells the reader nothing about how big the stranding risk is.

[reasoning_validity/major] D3 [verdict; CL8; K13; K14; counterarguments #1] The price-cut stress test (K12-K14, CL8, counterargument #1) assumes 100% utilization. A 45% cut on day one would raise break-even utilization to 0.0511/0.05544 = 92% for the Compute SP and 0.0457/0.05544 = 82% for the EC2 Instance SP. So at realistic utilization, a cut combined with under-use would wipe out the discount. 'Even a GPU-style 45% cut leaves both plans slightly ahead' and 'the price-cut risk is small next to utilization risk' therefore overstate how robust the result is. The draft never examines how price-cut risk and utilization risk interact.

[coverage/major] D5 [alternatives; C3] The draft leaves out obvious alternatives that a FinOps expert would weigh. (1) m7i-flex and m8i-flex: E9 says M8i-flex offers 5% lower prices, and m7i-flex is likewise priced below m7i. (2) Graviton m7g/m8g treated as a real option rather than a footnote: m7g.large at $0.0816 is about 19% cheaper per instance than m7i.large and appears only in practicalImplications. (3) Spot for interruptible portions of the workload. All three could change both the size of the commitment and which instance it should be bought for.

[reasoning_validity/major] D1 [C3 assessment; CL17; CL18; K24-K29; alternatives 'Compute SP', 'Move or test first'; tradeoffs[0]; counterarguments[1]] K24-K29 and CL17/CL18 express the Compute SP's post-migration cost 'per m7i-equivalent hour', as if a fixed $/hr commitment got cheaper when the workload moves to a faster family. A Savings Plan charges the committed $0.0511/hr whatever runs. The saving from moving only appears if the extra performance lets the requester run fewer instance-hours, or if the surplus coverage soaks up growth or other usage. For a single m7i.large, or any fleet that cannot be shrunk in fractional steps, moving to one m8i.large under a $0.0511 Compute SP costs more, not less. The SP rate would be about 0.0511*1.05 = $0.0537/hr, so the commitment covers only about 95% of the hour and the rest is billed at on-demand, giving about $0.056/hr against $0.0457 for staying on the m7i EC2 Instance SP. The same applies to the m7g case: at performance parity, a $0.0511 commitment covers about 1.24 m7g.large, so one migrated instance saves nothing. The draft never states this divisibility or fleet-scale assumption, yet the 5.6-month (K26) and 16-month (K29) payback windows and the 'commit on Graviton/M8i' advice depend on it.

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [CL20; alternatives 'Delay, or buy in staggered tranches'; tradeoffs[2]; practicalImplications[4]; verdict point (2)] CL20 and the 'Delay' alternative call waiting 'cheap insurance' and say the $40/instance-month cost of delay is 'small next to the risk of committing to the wrong family'. The draft's own figures say the opposite. Committing now on the m7i EC2 Instance SP instead of later on M8i costs about (0.0457-0.03999)*26,280 = about $150 per instance over the whole term (K9, K27), or about $4.2/month. Each month of delay costs about $40 (K35). Under the draft's own numbers, a delay of more than about 4 months costs more than the entire 36-month wrong-family penalty. The claim contradicts K25/K27, and the recommendation it supports (delay while deciding the family) is not justified as stated.

[reasoning_validity/major] D3 [C3 assessment conclusion; edgeCasesAndFailureModes[0]; alternatives 'EC2 Instance SP on m7i'] The cost of an m7i lock is framed only as a 'forgone gain' of about 2.2%, which assumes the workload can always keep running on m7i. If a move is forced, for example by a feature or capacity need, an architecture change, or a Graviton port that is actually carried out, an m7i-locked EC2 Instance SP or Standard RI is left stranded. The downside is then the whole remaining commitment, not 2.2% (the draft itself says there is no exit, E11). The edge cases and C3 conclusion understate this, which skews the EC2 Instance SP versus Compute SP recommendation.

[major/reviewer] D1 [verdict item (2); C3 assessment part (b); CL17; CL18; K24-K26, K29, K38, K39; alternatives 'Compute Savings Plan'; tradeoffs[0]] The 'divisible fleet' migration analysis gets wrong how a Savings Plan works. A Compute SP charges a fixed committed $/hr (here $0.0511 per original instance-equivalent) whether or not that coverage is used. If the requester moves to M8i and cuts instance-hours by about 1/1.2, their eligible usage at the SP rate falls to about $0.0447/hr, but they still pay $0.0511/hr. The unused $0.0064/hr is wasted. Cutting instance-hours therefore saves nothing under an existing commitment. The draft makes exactly this point for fixed fleets in K36, so it contradicts itself here. The per-unit figure of $0.0447 (K24), the 2.2% gain (K25), the roughly 6-month payback window (K26) and its 0-11 month sensitivity (K38, K39), and the 16-month Graviton window (K29) are only valid if the freed commitment is absorbed by workload growth or by other eligible usage. They are not valid simply because the fleet 'can shrink in proportion'. The arithmetic is correct, but the premise is false. As a result the verdict, CL17, CL18 and the Compute SP alternative all overstate the Compute SP's value for voluntary migration.

[major/reviewer] D2 [verdict item (2); C3 part (c); CL17; counterarguments[1]; tradeoffs[0]; practicalImplications[2]] The comparison of forced-move stranding ($1,201, K9) against the Compute SP premium ($142, K42) is not like-for-like, and the draft never turns it into a decision threshold. Suppose a forced move happens at t=0 under an EC2 Instance SP. The requester pays the stranded $1,201 plus full on-demand for the new family (about $2,781 for M8i at 0.1008x1.05x26,280), which is about $3,980 in total. Under a Compute SP they pay about $1,343 plus a small on-demand top-up (about $132), which is about $1,475. The real gap is about $2,500, not $1,201 against $142. The draft also never computes the forced-move probability at which the Compute SP premium pays for itself (roughly 6-12% depending on when the move happens). That threshold is the single most decision-useful number for choosing the plan type, and it can be computed from the packet's figures.
